README.md.text:
# S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker

Free, browser-only S corporation basis calculator. Type each year's K-1 figures
(contributions, loans, income, distributions, nondeductible expenses, losses) and it
carries **stock basis**, **debt basis** and **suspended losses** forward in the order
Form 7203 uses, flags **distributions that exceed basis**, restores debt basis
before stock basis after a loss year, and shows how much added basis would unlock a
suspended loss. Exports a CSV and a printable worksheet. Nothing is uploaded.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/s-corp-basis-tracker/

Open `index.html`. No build step, no dependencies. `node --test` runs the suite.

- `calc.mjs` - `step` (one year), `run` (roll forward), tolerant `parseYears` /
  `parseMoney`, `csv`, `packetHtml`.
- `parseBatch` / `runBatch` / `batchSummary` / `batchCsv` / `batchPacketHtml` - the
  preparer view: paste many shareholders at once (a `shareholder` column, plus an
  `opening` row for starting figures), get one summary with the shareholders needing
  attention first (excess distributions, suspended losses and gain on repaying reduced-basis loans each get a column and a flag), a combined CSV and one printable file with a worksheet each.
- `saleOutlook` - selling all your stock: gain on the shares against year-adjusted basis, the suspended loss a full sale would forfeit and the contribution that would deduct it first, and any loan face above its basis (section 5 on the page).
- `aaa` - the company's accumulated adjustments account year by year (section 6 on the page): income in, losses and nondeductible expenses out in the year they reduce basis, distributions paid from it, and the part paid beyond it. Tax-exempt income is left out.
- `fromK1Boxes` - type the Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) box numbers (`2024: 1=90000, 16D=60000, 16E=15000`, plus `contrib=` and `loan=`, which a K-1 does not show) and it fills the year table: boxes 1-10 split into income and loss by sign, 11 and 12 as deductions, 16A-16E as tax-exempt income, nondeductible expenses, distributions and loan repayments.
- `form-7203-basis-order.html` - the order basis is adjusted in, with a three-year
  worked example the test suite recomputes.
- `s-corp-distributions-over-basis.html` - when a distribution becomes taxable, three
  cases recomputed by the test suite.
- `s-corp-suspended-losses.html` - why a loss is suspended and what frees it, with a three-year example (loss, income, loan repayment) the test suite recomputes.
- `s-corp-loan-or-contribution-to-deduct-losses.html` - loan or capital contribution to unlock a suspended loss: same deduction, different repayment gain, with an example the test suite recomputes.
- `remember.mjs` - the opt-in "remember these entries on this device" box (off by default; browser storage only, erased by unticking or Clear), so next year's visit is one added line.
- `cli.mjs` - the same roll-forward in a terminal, for preparers who keep clients' K-1 figures in text files: `node cli.mjs years.csv`, `--k1` for K-1 box lines, `--batch` for many shareholders (needs-attention first), `--csv`, `--html`, `--json`, `--opening 20000,0,0,0`, `--example`. Zero dependencies, no network; tests in `cli.test.mjs`.
- `usage.mjs` - local-only feature counters with an opt-out.

The tests include a 4,000-year random check that basis is conserved on every step
and never goes negative.

## Host your own copy

Basis figures are financial detail, so you can serve the page from an address you control. It is a static site: the
server only hands out files and never sees a figure you type.

- **Docker:** `docker compose up -d`, then open <http://localhost:8080> (`Dockerfile` is nginx plus the page's files).
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile`, then `fly deploy` (`fly.toml`).
- **Render:** deploy from your fork with `render.yaml` (static site, no paid plan needed).
- Nothing runs on the author's accounts. The Docker image has not been built in the session that added these files,
  so build it once and open the page before relying on it. Tests: `node --test deploy.test.mjs`.

## What you use today, and what this does differently

- **A spreadsheet:** free, but the ordering (income, then distributions, then
  nondeductible expenses, then losses; debt basis restored before stock) is yours to
  get right, and nothing flags suspended losses.
- **Tax-software basis modules:** complete, but bundled with paid preparer software.
- **What this adds:** the roll-forward in Form 7203 order, suspended-loss and
  excess-distribution flags, and a worksheet to hand to a preparer, with no signup
  and no upload.

**No warranty.** Free and as-is; an organising aid, not tax or legal advice and not a
filed form. At-risk and passive-activity limits, the excess business loss limit, QBI,
the other adjustments account and earnings and profits from C corporation years, stock sales and state rules
are not modelled; a sale of stock is figured on the shares only. Check every figure against your K-1 and the Form 7203 instructions.
MIT licensed.

form-7203-basis-order.html.text:
S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker · free, in your browser

The order S corporation basis is adjusted in, with a three-year example

Form 7203 asks for your stock basis and debt basis in a fixed sequence. The sequence matters because basis cannot go below zero and each step uses what the one before it left.

  1. Add capital contributions and stock purchases, and the year's income items, including tax-exempt income. A new loan you make directly to the company adds debt basis.
  2. If debt basis was reduced by earlier losses, the year's net increase (income less distributions and nondeductible expenses) restores debt basis first, up to what you are still owed, and only then stock basis.
  3. Subtract distributions from stock basis, but not below zero. What is left over is the excess distribution.
  4. Subtract nondeductible expenses, again not below zero. Any excess carries forward.
  5. Subtract losses and deductions, including losses suspended from earlier years, first from stock basis and then from debt basis. What neither can absorb is suspended.
  6. Loan repayments come last. Repaying debt whose basis was reduced gives gain on the reduced share.

A worked example (invented)

A shareholder starts 2022 with $20,000 of stock basis and lends the company $30,000.

YearIncomeDistributionsLossResult
2022$0$0$70,000$1,500 of nondeductible expenses take stock to $18,500. The loss uses $18,500 of stock and $30,000 of debt basis; $21,500 is suspended.
2023$40,000$10,000$0The $30,000 net increase restores debt basis, then the $21,500 suspended loss is used against it. Stock basis ends at $0, debt basis at $8,500.
2024$90,500$60,000$0$21,500 of net increase restores debt basis first. After $2,000 of nondeductible expenses stock basis is $7,000; repaying $15,000 of the loan leaves debt basis of $15,000.

The same three rows are in the tracker's "Load an invented example" button, so you can change a number and watch the rest move.

Questions

Why does debt basis come back before stock basis?

When income follows a year of losses that ate into debt basis, the rules put the loan back to its face amount first, because that basis was used last. Only the remainder rebuilds stock basis.

Do losses or distributions come first?

Distributions. They reduce stock basis before nondeductible expenses and losses, so a loss in the same year cannot make a distribution tax free.

Can I just keep a spreadsheet?

Yes, if you follow the same order. The tracker applies it for you and checks that basis is conserved from step to step.

Open the tracker and put your own K-1 figures through it. Nothing is uploaded.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. Not legal, tax, financial or accounting advice; the example is invented and the rules are summarised from commonly published guidance that may be out of date. Check Form 7203 instructions and your K-1, or ask a tax professional.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These pages may be slow, moved or taken offline without notice.

index.html.text:
S-CORP SHAREHOLDER BASIS TRACKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Is my S corporation loss deductible, and is that distribution tax free?

Type in each year's K-1 figures. The tracker carries your stock basis, debt basis and suspended losses forward in the order Form 7203 uses, flags any distribution that exceeds basis, and shows how much basis would unlock a suspended loss.

An organising aid, not tax or legal advice, and not a filed form. Read the order basis is adjusted in, with a worked example what happens when distributions exceed basis, or why a loss is suspended and what frees it, or loan or capital contribution to deduct a loss, or which K-1 box feeds which line.

1. Where you start

Use the closing figures from your last basis worksheet, or what you paid for the stock if you are starting from the beginning. Leave blank for zero.

Have the Schedule K-1 in front of you?

Type each year's K-1 (Form 1120-S) box numbers instead of the columns below, one line per year, for example 2024: 1=90000, 4=200, 11=5000, 16A=500, 16C=2000, 16D=60000, 16E=15000. Boxes 1 to 10 are income, and a negative amount is a loss; boxes 11 and 12 are deductions; 16A and 16B tax-exempt income, 16C nondeductible expenses, 16D distributions, 16E loan repayments. The K-1 does not show what you contributed or lent, so add contrib= and loan=. Box numbers follow the current form; check them against yours.

2. One line per year

Columns, comma or tab separated: year, capital contributions and stock purchases, loans you made, loan repayments you received, income (negative is a loss), tax-exempt income, distributions, nondeductible expenses, losses and deductions. Amounts may use $, commas, (parentheses) or 1.5k.

Off by default. Kept only in this browser's own storage, never uploaded; untick it to erase them.

3. Result

4. Year-end planner for

Uses the last year you entered as the year still open. Change that row's distributions, contributions or loans and run again to test a decision.

5. Selling your stock?

Reads the last year you entered as the sale year (enter its income, distributions and losses through the sale date). Shows the gain on the shares and whether a loss would be lost.

6. Accumulated adjustments account (AAA)

The corporation's account of income it has already taxed to shareholders. Distributions out of it are not dividends even if the company has earnings from C corporation years. Uses the same years as above; tax-exempt income is not in it. Enter its balance from the company's Schedule M-2 (Form 1120-S) at the start, or leave blank for zero.

Preparing for several shareholders?

Paste a whole client list. Columns, comma or tab separated: shareholder, then the same columns as above starting with the year. A row with opening in the year column gives that shareholder's starting stock basis, debt basis, loan balance and suspended losses. You get one summary that puts the shareholders needing attention first, a combined CSV, and one printable file with a worksheet per shareholder.

Questions

What is S corporation shareholder basis?

It is your running tax investment in the S corporation: the stock basis (what you paid or contributed, plus your share of income, minus distributions and losses) and, separately, debt basis (money you lent the company directly). Basis decides how much of a K-1 loss you can deduct and how much of a distribution is tax free.

Do I need to file Form 7203?

Form 7203 generally goes with your return when you claim a deduction for an S corporation loss, receive a non-dividend distribution, dispose of stock, or receive a loan repayment, among other cases. Read the current instructions or ask your preparer; this tool only does the arithmetic in the same order.

What happens when my losses are bigger than my basis?

The excess is suspended, not lost. It carries forward indefinitely and becomes deductible in a later year when you add basis, through a stock purchase, a capital contribution, a direct loan from you to the company, or the company's own income.

Does a loan I personally guaranteed give me debt basis?

No. Debt basis comes from loans you made to the corporation yourself. Guaranteeing the company's bank loan, or lending through another entity, generally does not create it until you actually pay on the guarantee.

What if my distributions exceed my stock basis?

The excess is generally taxed as gain, capital gain if you held the stock more than a year. Distributions reduce stock basis before losses do, so a loss in the same year cannot make a distribution tax free.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The tracker runs in your browser. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and entries are only kept on your device, in this browser's own storage, if you tick the remember box, or in a file you save.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial or accounting advice and does not replace a tax professional or the instructions to Form 7203. It follows the commonly published ordering of basis adjustments and does not model at-risk limits, passive activity rules, the excess business loss limit, the qualified business income deduction, earnings and profits from C corporation years, the other adjustments account, stock sales, or state rules. Check every figure against your K-1 and your return.

Independent. Not affiliated with the IRS, any tax authority, or any tax software company, and none is named or ranked here. The example is invented.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record: nothing you enter is saved unless you tick the remember box, and that copy lives only in this browser, so download the CSV.

Everything runs in your browser. Your figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (basis_run, example_loaded, csv_downloaded, worksheet_downloaded, plan_viewed, sale_viewed, aaa_viewed, batch_run, batch_example_loaded, batch_csv_downloaded, batch_worksheets_downloaded, remember_on, k1_converted) are counted only in local storage on your device, never sent anywhere. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Related tools: the S corporation reasonable compensation calculator, the excess business loss calculator and the quarterly estimated tax calendar.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

s-corp-distributions-over-basis.html.text:
S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker · free, in your browser

When an S corporation distribution is more than your basis

A distribution from an S corporation is generally tax free up to your stock basis, then taxed as gain. Because basis is only known after the year's income is added, the same cash can be tax free or taxable depending on the year-end figures.

Two invented cases

Case 1. Stock basis at the start of the year is $10,000. The company earns nothing for you and distributes $25,000. $10,000 is tax free, basis falls to $0 and $15,000 is excess, generally capital gain if you have held the stock more than a year.

Case 2. Same start and same $25,000 distribution, but your share of income for the year is $20,000. Income is added first, so basis before the distribution is $30,000. Nothing is excess and basis ends at $5,000.

Case 3. Start at $10,000, distribute $10,000 and also have a $5,000 loss. The distribution takes basis to $0 first, so the $5,000 loss is suspended rather than deducted. The order costs you the deduction until basis returns.

What to check

  • If the company was ever a C corporation, a distribution beyond the accumulated adjustments account may be a dividend rather than gain. The tracker does not model that.
  • Distributions made early in the year are tested against year-end basis for the whole year, so timing within the year does not rescue them.
  • Adding a contribution or a direct loan before year end raises basis; ask a preparer how to document it.

Questions

Is an excess distribution always capital gain?

Generally it is treated as gain from the sale of the stock, capital gain if held over a year. Distributions of earnings from C corporation years can be dividends instead.

Does income earned later in the year count?

Yes. Your share of the year's income is added to basis before distributions are tested, even if the company earns it after the cash goes out.

Can I fix an excess distribution after year end?

Basis is measured at year end, so contributions made after year end do not count for that year. Talk to a tax professional about options before filing.

Open the tracker and put your own K-1 figures through it. Nothing is uploaded.

s-corp-k1-boxes-for-basis.html.text:
S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker · free, in your browser

Which K-1 box feeds which line of S corporation basis

Your Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S) never states your stock basis. It gives the year's amounts, and you carry basis forward yourself. This is where each box goes.

Box by box

K-1 boxWhat it isEffect on basis
1-10Ordinary business income, rental, interest, dividends, royalties, gains (a negative figure is a loss)Income raises basis; a loss is limited by basis
11, 12Section 179 and other deductionsTreated as losses
16A, 16BTax-exempt incomeRaises basis, untaxed
16CNondeductible expensesLowers basis, after distributions
16DDistributionsLowers basis; the part above basis is gain
16ERepayment of loans from shareholdersApplies to debt basis, not stock

The K-1 does not show money you contributed or lent during the year. Add those from your own records.

One invented year

You open 2024 with $30,000 of stock basis. Box 1 shows $50,000, box 16A $2,000, box 16C $3,000 and box 16D $20,000. Basis rises by $52,000 to $82,000, the $20,000 distribution is not taxed, and the $3,000 of nondeductible expenses comes off after it, so stock basis at year end is $59,000.

In the tracker, type 2024: 1=50000, 16A=2000, 16C=3000, 16D=20000 into the K-1 box entry and it fills the year table for you.

Questions

Which K-1 box is my S corporation stock basis?

None. The K-1 does not report your basis; you track it yourself from year to year. The K-1 gives the yearly amounts that raise or lower it, and Form 7203 is where the roll-forward is shown.

Do distributions in box 16D reduce my basis?

Yes, after income and other increases are added. A distribution up to your stock basis is not taxed; the part above it is taxed as a gain. Distributions come before nondeductible expenses and losses in the order basis is adjusted.

Does tax-exempt income in box 16A raise my basis?

Yes. Tax-exempt interest and similar income passes through untaxed but still increases stock basis, so leaving it out understates your basis.

Open the tracker and put your own K-1 figures through it. Nothing is uploaded. Related: the order basis is adjusted in and why a loss is suspended.

s-corp-loan-or-contribution-to-deduct-lo.text:
S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker · free, in your browser

S corp loan or capital contribution: which one unlocks a suspended loss?

When your share of an S corporation loss is bigger than your basis, the rest is suspended. You can free it by adding basis before the company's year ends, either as a capital contribution or as a direct loan from you to the company. Both give the same deduction this year. They are not the same afterwards.

One invented example

You start the year with $5,000 of stock basis and no loans to the company. Your share of the loss is $30,000. With nothing added you deduct $5,000 and $25,000 is suspended.

Option A: contribute $25,000 before year end

Stock basis becomes $30,000, the loss fits, and you deduct $30,000. Stock basis and debt basis are both $0 at year end and nothing is suspended. The $25,000 is capital in the company, not a balance owed to you.

Option B: lend the company $25,000 before year end

The loan has $25,000 of basis from the day it is made, so the loss fits and you deduct $30,000. The company still owes you $25,000, but the loss used all of that loan's basis, so its basis is $0.

Where they differ: getting money back

Next year the company repays the $25,000. With a basis of $0 the whole repayment is $25,000 of gain (ordinary income if the loan is a note, capital gain if it is an open account). If the company earns $10,000 first, income restores loan basis before anything else, so the same repayment gives $15,000 of gain.

Deduction this yearOwed to you afterGain if repaid next year with no income
Contribute $25,000$30,000$0not repayable as debt
Lend $25,000$30,000$25,000$25,000

So a loan keeps a claim on the money, but taking it back is taxed to the extent losses used its basis. A contribution gives up the claim. Neither changes the deduction.

What to check

  • Only a direct loan from you counts. Guaranteeing a bank loan does not add basis.
  • Document a loan as one: a written note, a rate and a repayment plan. Whether it is debt is a question of facts; a preparer should decide.
  • The deduction can still be limited by at-risk and passive-activity rules after basis. The tracker does not model them.

Questions

Should I make a loan or a capital contribution to deduct an S corporation loss?

Either adds the basis the loss needs, and the deduction is the same. The difference comes later. A contribution is not repaid. A direct loan can be repaid, but a loan whose basis losses have used is returned with gain on the reduced part. Which fits depends on whether you expect to take the money back, and how the loan is documented; ask a preparer.

Does a bank loan I guarantee give me basis to deduct an S corporation loss?

Generally no. Only money you put in yourself counts: stock purchases, capital contributions, and a direct loan from you to the company. Guaranteeing a loan from a bank or lending through another entity generally does not.

Does the contribution have to be made before year end?

Basis for the loss limit is tested at the end of the company's tax year, so money added after year end counts toward the next year, not the year that was limited.

Open the tracker: its year-end planner shows the contribution or loan that would deduct your own suspended loss. Nothing is uploaded. Related: why a loss is suspended, the order basis is adjusted in and distributions over basis.

s-corp-suspended-losses.html.text:
S-Corp Shareholder Basis Tracker · free, in your browser

Why an S corporation loss is suspended, and what frees it

An S corporation passes its loss to you, but you can deduct it only up to your basis: stock basis first, then the basis in loans you made to the company directly. What does not fit is suspended and carried forward. Repaying a loan whose basis was used up is where a later surprise comes from.

One invented example, three years

2024. You start with $20,000 of stock basis and lend the company $10,000. Your share of the loss is $40,000. It uses all $20,000 of stock basis and then the $10,000 of loan basis, so you deduct $30,000 and $10,000 is suspended. The loan is still owed to you at $10,000 but its basis is $0.

2025. Your share of income is $4,000. Income first restores the loan's reduced basis, then it absorbs the suspended loss, so $6,000 is still suspended at year end and the loan basis is back to $0.

2026. The company repays the $10,000 loan. With a basis of $0 the whole repayment is gain: $10,000 of gain (ordinary income if the loan is a note, capital gain if it is an open account), and the $6,000 loss is still suspended.

What to check

  • Only money you put in yourself counts. A bank loan you guarantee does not raise your basis.
  • Basis is tested at year end for losses, so a contribution made after year end counts for the next year, not the one that was limited.
  • At-risk and passive-activity rules can limit a loss after basis does. The tracker does not model them.

Questions

Do suspended S corporation losses expire?

No. They carry forward indefinitely for as long as you hold stock, and become deductible in a year when your basis is increased enough to absorb them. Losses still suspended when your stock is sold or the company ends are generally lost.

Does a loan I made to the S corporation give me basis?

Only a direct loan from you to the company, at face value, gives debt basis. Guaranteeing a bank loan or lending through another entity generally does not. Ask a preparer how your loan is documented.

Why did repaying my shareholder loan create taxable income?

If losses already reduced the loan's basis, repaying it returns more cash than the basis you have left, and the reduced part is gain. Income in later years restores loan basis first, which is why the order matters.
